profile.campus: Evocative South Bay / Silicon Valley cluster (with SJC14, SJC7)

source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

profile.address: 2151 Mission College Blvd, Santa Clara, CA 95054
profile.reading:
Per Evocative's own site, this Santa Clara, California facility, designated SJC11, sits at 2151 Mission College Boulevard and totals 73,000 square feet, drawing 9 megawatts of total power capacity delivered as two 4.5 megawatt feeds from diverse substations. Evocative describes the mechanical plant as two 1,200 ton Baltimore Air Coil cooling units backed by four 75 horsepower pumps, a five unit, 750 kVA UPS system arranged N plus 1, and four 1.5 megawatt Caterpillar generators for backup, and it markets the building as a Tier 3 design facility. The operator's own page states this building was originally an Intel network operations center and satellite facility that has since been completely updated for colocation use, and it puts roughly 11.9 million people within 100 miles of the site.

Evocative lists compliance with HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, ISAE 3402, SSAE 18, LEED, and Green Globes standards for this building, and names a broad carrier roster on site including AT&T, Lumen, Cogent, Comcast, Verizon, Zayo, Megaport, Bandwidth IG, Spectrum, and PacketFabric, alongside its own Evocative IP network and a listed interconnection to Silicon Valley Power, the municipal utility that also supplies the building's electric service. The company describes direct fiber connectivity to San Francisco in addition to that carrier list, and 24 hour access control, surveillance, and monitoring.

Evocative describes itself as a global infrastructure provider operating data center, bare metal, network, cloud, and managed services across 24 data centers in 14 metros, with this Santa Clara building one of two Evocative facilities in the South Bay alongside a separate SJC14 building elsewhere in the market. Santa Clara is headquarters to Intel Corporation and sits at the center of Silicon Valley's dense data center and technology corridor, alongside major colocation campuses operated by Equinix, Digital Realty, and CoreSite in the same city. The area draws power from Silicon Valley Power, the city owned municipal utility, and from Pacific Gas and Electric in surrounding areas, both interconnected to the CAISO grid that also serves much of central and northern California. Evocative has built part of its portfolio through acquisitions of smaller regional colocation operators, consolidating facilities like this former Intel site into a unified network under the Evocative name, a pattern consistent with the building's history as purpose built Intel infrastructure repurposed for third party colocation rather than constructed from the ground up as a commercial data center.

No tenant is named for this facility in any source reviewed, and no per rack or per square foot power density figure is published beyond the total 9 megawatt, dual 4.5 megawatt feed capacity described above.

profile.reading: Evocative Secaucus, branded EWR1 on the operator's own site, is a data center in Secaucus, New Jersey. Evocative's own dedicated page for this facility, fetched directly from evocative.com, gives an address of 1 Enterprise Avenue N, Secaucus, New Jersey 07094, superseding this row's earlier reverse geocoded approximation, and describes a 105,000 square foot facility with 10 megawatts of total power capacity delivered as two 5 megawatt diverse underground feeds, expandable to 20 megawatts. The operator's own page lists 4 x 400 ton air cooled chillers in an N+1 design, 4 x 1.4 megawatt APC Symmetra UPS systems, and 4 x 2 megawatt generators in an N+1 configuration rated for 48 hours at full load. The page states the site sits outside the 500 year flood plain and within 100 miles of approximately 31.2 million people, and describes direct fiber access to a nearby Equinix campus less than a mile away. Evocative's own page lists compliance with HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, ISAE 3402, and SSAE 18 standards. Evocative describes itself elsewhere on its site as a global infrastructure provider operating data center, bare metal, network, cloud, and managed services across 24 data centers in 14 strategically located metros and 32 points of presence, with this Secaucus building serving the New York metro market alongside other Evocative locations in California, Arizona, Georgia, Massachusetts, Texas, and Washington already on file elsewhere in this registry. Secaucus sits in the Hudson County data center corridor across the river from Manhattan, a market anchored by major carrier hotel and colocation campuses including Equinix's Secaucus buildings and other operators drawn by proximity to New York financial and media firms along with lower New Jersey real estate and power costs relative to Manhattan itself.

profile.address: 1807, Michael Faraday Court, Reston Station, Reston, Fairfax County, Virginia, 20190
profile.reading:
Evocative IAD1 occupies a single building at 1807 Michael Faraday Court in Reston, Virginia, an address the operator's own current facility page confirms alongside a description of the site as a Tier III edge data center with two 200 kVA redundant utility transformers, roughly 400 kVA of total electrical service, and 14 thirty ton CRAC cooling units. That operator confirmed detail describes a comparatively small, edge oriented building rather than a hyperscale campus, consistent with the site's documented history.

The building's ownership history stretches back decades and is unusually well documented in trade press. Data Center Knowledge reported that the facility, built in 1982, was originally an AboveNet property before Digital Realty Trust acquired it in 2006. Digital Realty later sold a larger multi state portfolio including this Reston property to Netrality Properties, and Netrality in turn sold the Virginia assets, including this building and a second former Digital Realty site at 251 Exchange Place in Herndon, to Lincoln Property Company's Lincoln Rackhouse division, in a transaction Data Center Knowledge dated to July 2016. At that time Lincoln Rackhouse described the Reston building as having just over 11,000 square feet of raised floor space and about 1 megawatt of power capacity, up from 900 kilowatts, with the building then only partially occupied.

Evocative, led at the time by chief executive Arman Khalili, entered a long term lease with an option to purchase the property from Lincoln Rackhouse, announced in January 2018 per both Data Center Knowledge and Data Center Dynamics, marking the company's first East Coast facility after earlier 2018 West Coast acquisitions from 365 Data Centers and ColoNet. Those January 2018 trade press reports described the Reston facility's capacity at that time as 25,000 square feet and 2.2 megawatts, expandable to 53,000 square feet and 5.7 megawatts as demand grew. Those trade press figures for overall building capacity do not obviously reconcile with the smaller 400 kVA total electrical service figure stated on Evocative's own current site for this building, and this registry has not been able to resolve that discrepancy from public sources, so both are recorded here rather than one being silently preferred over the other.

Evocative's own site describes itself as a global infrastructure provider operating data center, bare metal, network, cloud, and managed services across 24 data centers in 14 metros and 32 points of presence, claiming SOC 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SSAE 18, and ISAE 3402 compliance across its facilities and a carrier neutral posture at this Reston site specifically. The building sits in Reston, Virginia, near the Dulles Technology Corridor and within reach of the dense Ashburn, Virginia colocation and hyperscale cluster that handles a large share of North American internet traffic, though this smaller edge facility is a different class of building from the larger wholesale campuses further out toward Loudoun County. No Fairfax County rezoning or special exception case specific to 1807 Michael Faraday Court was located in this research, plausibly because the building predates modern data center specific zoning categories and has changed hands and operators repeatedly without new construction requiring such review. No square footage or year built figure newer than the trade press history above was found on Evocative's own page, and no county assessor record was consulted this session, so current occupied square footage and any standby or onsite generation capacity remain unconfirmed.

reading.body:
Evocative operates a single confirmed facility with published power capacity: Santa Clara, California, with 9 MW across 73,000 square feet, while two additional US locations lack published capacity figures.

The operator describes itself as a colocation provider with 10 US data centers spanning seven states and eight international points of presence. Its CEO since February 2017, Arman Khalili, came from founding two prior infrastructure companies and leading Black Lotus before its acquisition by Level 3 Communications. Under Khalili, Evocative acquired Emeryville and San Jose facilities from 365 Data Centers around 2017, notably repurchasing Emeryville after selling it to 365 Main in 2013. The company's expansion pattern reflects consolidation common in colocation, where facilities rotate between operators rather than new construction.

The Santa Clara facility holds dual 4.5 MW feeds from separate substations and maintains SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, SSAE 18, LEED, and Green Globes certifications. At 9 MW total for 73,000 square feet, this yields approximately 0.123 MW per thousand square feet, typical for colocation serving enterprise rather than hyperscale workloads. Neither the New Jersey nor Virginia facilities had published capacity or square footage at the time of research, limiting visibility into Evocative's true power footprint.

The registry entry here covers only three locations. Evocative's stated portfolio of ten US data centers means seven remain untracked, and the Virginia facility does not appear on the operator's own site, indicating either stale registry data or a location the company no longer lists or serves. Without headquarters address, founding year, or current ownership information from primary sources, financial trajectory and current capitalization remain opaque.
